panels.rationale: The image is an MRI of the head showing hyperintense basal ganglia lesions on T2-weighted images in a child. This radiological finding is strongly associated with kernicterus, as supported by the article title and text. The panel is a real patient image and displays a key clinical manifestation.

in_text_mentions: Upon admission the patient presented total bilirubin values of 42.6 mg/dl (41.8 mg/dl from indirect bilirubin), 11.8 g/dl hemoglobin, 8% reticulocytes, O (Rh+) and B (Rh+) blood types for child and mother, respectively, and negative direct Coombs. G6PD testing was reported as deficient, and the quantification of the serum levels of this enzyme was 0.278 U/gHb (normal value range 4.6 to 13.5 U/gHb). Cranial magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated hyperintense basal ganglia lesions on T2-weighted images (Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: An axial T2-weighted image showing hyperintensity in globus pallidus bilaterally (arrows), a typical finding in chronic bilirubin encephalopathy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is an axial T2-weighted brain MRI showing bilateral hyperintensity in the globus pallidus, which is a specific, classic radiological finding of chronic kernicterus sequelae. B: Panel B is an axial T2 DRIVE image showing tissue loss in both hippocampi. While not in the provided finding vocabulary, hippocampal atrophy is a recognized and described sequela of kernicterus, including in-text mentions of hippocampal atrophy and T2 hyperintensity in the basal nuclei. C: Panel C is included as part of the figure set depicting the evolution and sequelae of kernicterus. It provides the anatomical context for the tissue loss described in panel B, showing the lack of signal in previously affected areas.
panels.attribution_text: Resaz et al. The Importance of Neuroimaging Follow-Up in Bilirubin-Induced Encephalopathy: A Clinical Case Review.. Brain sciences 2025. doi:10.3390/brainsci15060539. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Brain MRI obtained at 6 months. (A) An axial T2-weighted image showing hyperintensity in globus pallidus bilaterally (arrows), a typical finding in chronic bilirubin encephalopathy; (B) an axial T2 DRIVE image showing tissue loss in both hippocampi (arrowheads), corresponding to the areas that previously showed T1 hyperintensity (see Figure 1) which are no longer detectable on a T1-weighted image (C).
in_text_mentions: The exam was repeated at two months of life, showing partial resolution of the previously described alterations, and again at six months of age, revealing T2-weighted hyperintensity in both globi pallidi and hippocampal atrophy (Figure 2). Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) of the basal nuclei showed a minimal reduction in N-acetylaspartate (NAA) levels. These neuroradiological findings were compatible with sequelae of kernicterus.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels ((a), (b), (c), (d)). (a): Shows yellowish discoloration in the subthalamic nucleus and hippocampus, a known manifestation of kernicterus. (b): Shows discoloration in the specified brainstem and cerebellar regions consistent with kernicterus findings. (c): Shows pigment accumulation in choroid plexus cells, documented in the context of the case. (d): Shows Alzheimer's type II astrocytes, a pathological finding cited in the context of this patient's illness.

panels.figure_caption: Neuropathologic findings from a patient with kernicterus. (a) Yellowish discoloration of subthalamic nucleus and hippocampus; (b) discoloration of medullary tegmentum, inferior olives, and cerebellar tonsils; (c) cytoplasmic pigment in cells of choroid plexus (20× magnification); (d) Alzheimer’s type II astrocytes (arrow) in keeping with liver failure (20× magnification).
in_text_mentions: subthalamic nucleus may also display atrophy. Classic full-blown kernicterus typically leads to yellow discoloration of the basal ganglia, especially the globus pallidus, and subthalamic nucleus (see Figure 1). Other susceptible areas include the thalamus, mammillary bodies, CA2 sector of the hippocampus, subiculum, indusium griseum, and uncus. Vulnerable areas in the brainstem include the substantia nigra, oculomotor nucleus, trochlear nucleus, cochlear nucleus, vestibular nucleus, inferior colliculus, and superior olivary complex. lar cytoplasm, often with microvacuolation and the disruption of neuronal and nuclear membranes. Yellow pigment can be prominent within the neuronal cytoplasm. By the end of the first week, dissolution of affected neurons becomes apparent, and nuclear and plasma membranes become poorly defined. In subsequent days to weeks, neuronal loss, often with mineralization, and astrocytosis can be observed. As in other causes of liver injury, Alzheimer’s type II astrocytes (Figure 1d) can be found throughout the deep grey matter structures, as well as the neocortex, brainstem, and cerebellum [43,44,45].
